clinicalPearls: Results from chronic ocular hypoperfusion, almost always due to severe ipsilateral internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion, occasionally ophthalmic artery disease.

Typical presentation is subacute, progressive monocular visual loss with a dull ocular or periorbital ache sometimes called ocular angina, and prolonged visual recovery after exposure to bright light.

Anterior segment signs include episcleral and conjunctival congestion, corneal oedema, mild anterior chamber inflammation and iris neovascularisation (rubeosis), which may progress to neovascular glaucoma.
Intraocular pressure may be paradoxically normal or low despite neovascular glaucoma, because ciliary body hypoperfusion reduces aqueous production.

Posterior segment shows narrowed retinal arteries, dilated but characteristically non-tortuous veins, mid-peripheral dot-and-blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms and sometimes spontaneous retinal arterial pulsation.

The dilated-but-not-tortuous veins and mid-peripheral rather than posterior-pole haemorrhages help distinguish it from central retinal vein occlusion, and it is also an important mimic of diabetic retinopathy.
It is a marker of severe systemic atherosclerosis carrying a high risk of stroke and cardiac death, so urgent vascular and cardiovascular assessment is mandatory.

Ocular treatment (panretinal photocoagulation, anti-VEGF therapy, glaucoma control) addresses neovascular complications, whereas carotid revascularisation is directed mainly at systemic risk and visual outcomes remain guarded.
reference.pathophysiology: Severe stenosis or occlusion of the internal or common carotid artery, and occasionally the ophthalmic artery, lowers perfusion pressure to the eye below the threshold needed to sustain retinal and anterior segment metabolism. Chronic ischaemia and hypoxia upregulate vascular endothelial growth factor and other angiogenic mediators, driving neovascularisation of the iris, drainage angle and retina. Reduced ocular perfusion pressure produces venous stasis with dilated veins, dot-and-blot haemorrhages and microaneurysms, while arterial narrowing reflects the diminished inflow. Hypoperfusion of the ciliary body reduces aqueous humour formation, which can mask the pressure rise otherwise expected with neovascular glaucoma. Because the eye subsists on a critically low perfusion reserve, small further falls in systemic blood pressure or ocular perfusion can precipitate ischaemic symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Central retinal vein occlusion, both ischaemic and non-ischaemic
Central or branch retinal artery occlusion
Giant cell arteritis or other vasculitis causing ocular ischaemia
Aortic arch disease (Takayasu arteritis) or dissection reducing ocular inflow
Anterior uveitis accounting for the anterior segment inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Carotid duplex ultrasound to assess stenosis or occlusion
CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography, of the carotid and cerebral vessels
Fundus fluorescein angiography showing delayed choroidal filling, prolonged arteriovenous transit and late vessel staining
Slit-lamp examination with gonioscopy for rubeosis and angle neovascularisation, plus intraocular pressure measurement
Dilated fundus examination with optical coherence tomography for macular oedema
Cardiovascular and stroke risk assessment including blood pressure, lipids, glucose and cardiac evaluation
Inflammatory markers to exclude giant cell arteritis where relevant
redFlags: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) or other transient ischaemic attack or stroke symptoms indicating high stroke risk
Iris neovascularisation or established neovascular glaucoma
Features suggesting giant cell arteritis such as headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness
Bilateral involvement suggesting severe or proximal aortic arch disease
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is guarded, particularly once neovascular glaucoma develops. The syndrome signals severe systemic vascular disease with a substantial risk of stroke and cardiac death, so systemic prognosis often dominates management.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as ordinary central retinal vein occlusion and missing the underlying carotid disease.
Being falsely reassured by a normal or low intraocular pressure despite florid neovascular glaucoma.
Failing to arrange urgent vascular and cardiovascular workup, as the syndrome is a systemic red flag.
Overlooking giant cell arteritis as a treatable cause of ocular ischaemia in older patients.
Expecting carotid revascularisation to restore vision, when its main benefit is systemic risk reduction and it can occasionally worsen glaucoma.
management: Treatment of the underlying carotid occlusive disease with carotid endarterectomy or stenting for significant stenosis, in conjunction with vascular surgery
Aggressive systemic vascular risk reduction with antiplatelet therapy, statins and control of hypertension, diabetes and smoking to reduce the high risk of stroke and cardiac death
Panretinal photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for iris, angle and retinal neovascularisation
Management of neovascular glaucoma with topical intraocular-pressure-lowering agents and, where needed, cyclodestructive or glaucoma drainage surgery
Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for associated macular oedema
Urgent multidisciplinary referral to stroke, vascular surgery and cardiology services alongside ophthalmology
Regular ophthalmic surveillance with gonioscopy and intraocular pressure monitoring to detect progressive neovascularisation early
